concepts.name: Fork
concepts.one_liner: One piece attacks two things at once, and only one of them can run.
concepts.teaching:
A fork is the simplest way to win material, and it is the first tactic most
players learn to see. One piece attacks two targets simultaneously; the
opponent can answer only one threat per move, so the other target falls.

Knights fork most famously, because their move is the one no other piece can
block or imitate — a knight on the right square attacks in a shape nothing
else covers. But every piece forks. Pawns fork by advancing into two
captures. Queens fork along two lines at once. Kings fork in the endgame,
which is part of why an active king matters so much once the queens leave.

The practical skill is not spotting a fork that already exists; it is
noticing that two enemy pieces *stand on a forkable geometry* and then
working out how to get a piece to that square with tempo.

concepts.name: Pin
concepts.one_liner: A piece cannot move because something more valuable sits behind it.
concepts.teaching:
A pin freezes a piece by putting something it must protect directly behind
it on the same line. Only the long-range pieces can pin: bishop, rook, queen.

The distinction that matters is between an *absolute* pin, where the piece
behind is the king and moving is therefore illegal, and a *relative* pin,
where moving is legal but loses material. Absolute pins are permanent until
the geometry changes. Relative pins can be broken whenever the owner decides
the cost is worth paying — which is exactly why a relative pin is a weaker
grip than it looks.

A pinned piece is a defender that cannot defend. The standard follow-up is
not to win the pinned piece directly but to pile more attackers onto it, or
to attack whatever it was guarding, since it can no longer step in.

concepts.name: Skewer
concepts.one_liner: A pin in reverse — the valuable piece is in front and must move.
concepts.teaching:
A skewer attacks a valuable piece through to a lesser one behind it. The
front piece is forced to move, and the piece behind it is captured.

Geometrically it is identical to a pin; only the order of the targets is
swapped. That makes them easy to confuse and worth separating deliberately:
a pin *immobilises*, a skewer *forces movement*. A pin is a long-term
positional asset you can build on. A skewer usually resolves immediately.

The most common practical skewer is a check along a rank, file, or diagonal
that wins a rook or queen standing behind the king.

concepts.name: Discovered Attack
concepts.one_liner: Move one piece out of the way and the piece behind it does the work.
concepts.teaching:
A discovered attack unmasks a line. The piece that moves and the piece that
attacks are different, which is what makes these so easy to miss — you are
looking at the wrong piece.

Their power comes from a doubling of threats. The moving piece is free to
create a threat of its own while the unmasked piece creates another, so a
discovery generates two threats from one move. Nothing else in chess does
that as cheaply.

Because the moving piece is unconstrained, it can go somewhere apparently
absurd — including somewhere it can be captured — as long as the discovered
threat is bigger than whatever it gives up.

concepts.name: Discovered Check
concepts.one_liner: A discovery where the unmasked line gives check, so the reply is forced.
concepts.teaching:
A discovered check is a discovered attack whose unmasked line hits the king.
That single detail changes everything, because check must be answered
immediately. The moving piece can therefore do something the opponent would
normally never permit — capture a defended queen, or step onto a square
attacked by three pieces — and there is nothing to be done about it that
turn.

This is the tactic that most often produces material gain that looks like it
should be impossible.

concepts.name: Double Check
concepts.one_liner: Two pieces check at once, so only a king move can answer.
concepts.teaching:
In a double check, the moving piece gives check *and* uncovers a second
checking piece. Both attack the king at once.

This matters because of a quirk of the rules: you may block a check or
capture the checking piece, but you cannot do either against two checkers on
two different lines with one move. The king *must* move. No block, no
capture, no interposition.

That is why double check is the engine behind so many famous mating
combinations — it strips the defender of every option except one, and if the
king has no squares, it is mate regardless of how much material is standing
around doing nothing.

concepts.name: Deflection
concepts.one_liner: Force a defender away from the job it is doing.
concepts.teaching:
A defender is only a defender while it stays where it is. Deflection makes
it an offer it cannot refuse — usually a check or a capture of something
bigger — and once it has stepped away, whatever it was guarding falls.

The mental move is to stop looking at what you can capture and start asking
what is *holding the position together*. Identify the piece doing the
defensive work, then look for anything that makes it move.

Deflection and decoy are close relatives and often confused. Deflection
drags a piece *away from* a duty. Decoy lures a piece *onto* a specific
square.

concepts.name: Decoy
concepts.one_liner: Lure a piece onto a square where it can be hit.
concepts.teaching:
A decoy — Lichess tags these as "attraction" — pulls an enemy piece onto a
particular square, usually with a sacrifice it is obliged to accept, so that
a follow-up tactic works against it there.

The classic pattern drags the king onto a square where a knight can fork it
against the queen, or onto an open file where a rook waits. The material
given up is irrelevant if the resulting geometry wins more.

Where deflection asks "what would make that defender leave?", decoy asks
"which square do I wish that piece were standing on?" and then works out
what price would put it there.

concepts.name: Clearance
concepts.one_liner: Vacate a square or line your own piece needs, often with tempo.
concepts.teaching:
Sometimes the obstacle is your own. Clearance moves one of your pieces out
of the way — frequently sacrificing it — so that a square, file, or diagonal
opens for another of your pieces.

These are hard to see because the move looks like a blunder. A piece steps
onto a defended square, or is simply given away, and the point is not what
it does there but what it stops blocking.

Clearance almost always has to come with tempo. Give the opponent a free
move and they will use it to cover the square you just spent a piece to open.

concepts.name: Interference
concepts.one_liner: Cut the line between a defender and what it defends.
concepts.teaching:
Interference plants a piece — usually a sacrificed one — directly on the
line between an enemy defender and the thing it is protecting. The defender
is still on the board and still pointing the right way, but the connection
is severed.

This is among the rarest and most beautiful tactics, because the
interfering piece is often *en prise* to two different pieces and it does
not matter: whichever one captures it, the other stops defending.

Interference is the mirror image of clearance. Clearance opens a line you
want; interference closes a line they need.

concepts.name: X-Ray
concepts.one_liner: A piece attacks or defends straight through another piece.
concepts.teaching:
An x-ray is an attack or a defence that operates *through* an intervening
piece — the influence is latent, and becomes real the moment the piece in
between moves or is captured.

The defensive version is the more useful one to know. A rook can "defend"
a piece through an enemy rook: if the enemy captures, you recapture, because
your defence was pointing at the square all along.

Learning to see x-rays mostly means learning to evaluate captures on a
square by counting *every* piece pointed at it, not just the ones with a
clear path today.

concepts.name: Zwischenzug
concepts.one_liner: Before recapturing, insert a bigger threat.
concepts.teaching:
A zwischenzug — an in-between move — interrupts what looked like a forced
sequence. Instead of making the "obvious" recapture, you insert a move
carrying a larger threat, force a response, and only then go back and
recapture.

Every player has lost material to one, because exchanges feel automatic. He
takes, I take back. The zwischenzug exists precisely in that gap: the
recapture is not going anywhere, so if there is something more urgent
available first, play it first.

The habit worth building: before any recapture, ask once whether a check or
a bigger threat exists. It costs a second and it catches the whole family.

concepts.name: Back-Rank Mate
concepts.one_liner: A king trapped behind its own unmoved pawns is mated on the first rank.
concepts.teaching:
After castling, the king sits behind three pawns that have never moved. Very
comfortable — until a rook or queen arrives on the back rank, at which point
those pawns are a wall the king cannot climb.

The threat shapes far more games than the mate itself. Because back-rank
mate is always latent, defenders spend tempi on it: giving the king an
escape square, keeping a rook home, or having to answer a check they would
otherwise ignore. Attackers exploit it indirectly, since any defender on the
back rank is doing two jobs and can therefore be deflected.

The prophylactic move — pushing a rook's pawn one square to make an escape
hatch — is one of the highest-value non-moves in chess.

concepts.name: Smothered Mate
concepts.one_liner: A knight mates a king that its own pieces have boxed in.
concepts.teaching:
A king surrounded entirely by its own pieces has no flight squares, and the
one piece that can reach it anyway is the knight, since it jumps.

The full pattern, Philidor's Legacy, is worth memorising as a unit: queen
checks on the diagonal, king goes to the corner, knight checks, king returns,
queen sacrifices herself on g8 to *force* the rook to capture and fill the
last escape square, and the knight delivers mate on f7. The queen sacrifice
is a decoy whose purpose is to make the defender block its own king.

It is the clearest illustration in chess that material and safety are
different things.

concepts.name: Removing the Defender
concepts.one_liner: Capture the piece that was holding everything together.
concepts.teaching:
The bluntest way to beat a defended target is to take the defender. No
finesse required — just recognition.

This is the concept that teaches the counting habit that underlies all
tactics. Before assessing whether a capture works, list every attacker and
every defender of the square, then ask what happens to that count if you
remove one of them.

Where deflection persuades a defender to leave and interference cuts it off,
this simply takes it. It is the most common of the three by a wide margin.

concepts.name: Hanging Piece
concepts.one_liner: An undefended piece is a tactic waiting to happen.
concepts.teaching:
A hanging piece is simply one that is undefended. Sometimes it can be taken
outright. Far more often, its real cost is indirect: an undefended piece is
what makes forks, skewers, discoveries, and in-between moves work.

The strongest players do not so much calculate tactics as notice that the
preconditions for one exist. Loose pieces are the single most reliable
precondition. There is an old coaching line for it — *loose pieces drop off*
— and it is less a joke than a search heuristic.

The practical version, for both sides: after every opponent move, note which
pieces on both sides are undefended. Most tactical opportunities and most
blunders live in that list.

concepts.name: Trapped Piece
concepts.one_liner: A piece with no safe squares can be hunted down at leisure.
concepts.teaching:
A piece that has wandered too far, or been walled in by pawns, can be
attacked and won even though nothing is hanging right now — because it has
nowhere to go.

Bishops are the usual victims. A bishop that grabs a wing pawn frequently
finds the retreat squares covered by pawns that were always going to advance
anyway. Knights on the rim get trapped similarly.

Trapping is slower than most tactics, which is why it is missed: the win
takes two or three quiet moves rather than one forcing sequence. Look for it
whenever an enemy piece is deep in your position and its escape routes are
few.

concepts.name: Quiet Move
concepts.one_liner: The winning move is not a check or a capture — it is a threat nothing can meet.
concepts.teaching:
Most tactics are forcing. A quiet move is the exception that makes strong
players strong: no check, no capture, no immediate threat to anything, and
yet the position is now lost for the opponent because every answer fails.

They are hard for humans and were historically hard for engines, because
the natural search order examines checks and captures first. A quiet move is
invisible to that search.

Typically a quiet move creates an unstoppable threat, or removes the
opponent's only counterplay before cashing in. When a position feels winning
but every forcing line comes up short, the answer is usually a quiet move.

concepts.name: Underpromotion
concepts.one_liner: Sometimes a knight — or a rook — beats a queen.
concepts.teaching:
Promoting to a queen is right almost always, which is exactly why the
exceptions are so easy to miss.

Two reasons to underpromote. First, the knight moves in a way the queen
cannot: promoting to a knight can deliver check or a fork that a new queen
simply does not attack. Second, avoiding stalemate: a new queen may leave
the enemy king with no legal move, throwing away a win, where a rook keeps
a square free and mates next move.

It is a small category, but it is the clearest demonstration that piece
value is contextual rather than absolute.

concepts.name: En Passant
concepts.one_liner: The capture that expires if you do not take it immediately.
concepts.teaching:
When a pawn advances two squares and lands beside an enemy pawn, that pawn
may capture it as though it had advanced only one — but only on the very
next move. Wait, and the right is gone permanently.

The rule exists to close a loophole created when the two-square first move
was introduced: without it, a pawn could slip past an enemy pawn untouched.

It matters more than its rarity suggests, because it is the one capture
players forget exists. Defensive calculations quietly assume a pawn is safe
when it is not, and endgames turn on a capture nobody counted.

concepts.name: Sacrifice
concepts.one_liner: Give up material for something worth more than material.
concepts.teaching:
A sacrifice trades material for something else: time, an open line, the
safety of the enemy king, a square. It is not generosity and it is not a
gamble — a sound sacrifice is a calculation whose payoff is simply denominated
in a different currency.

Worth separating the true sacrifice from the sham. A sham sacrifice is a
forced sequence that regains the material with interest — really just a
combination, and verifiable to the end. A true sacrifice cannot be
calculated to a clear conclusion, and rests on judgement about the resulting
position.

Almost every sacrifice you will actually play is a sham sacrifice. Those are
the ones worth training, because they can be checked.

concepts.name: The f7 Square
concepts.one_liner: f7 and f2 are defended only by the king, and every opening fight knows it.
concepts.teaching:
At the start of the game, f7 for Black and f2 for White are defended by
exactly one piece: the king. Every other pawn near the king has support from
a piece; those two do not.

This asymmetry drives an enormous amount of opening theory. It is why the
bishop goes to c4, why the knight jumps to g5, why the Fried Liver exists,
and why a great many short games between beginners end the same way.

Understanding it defensively is worth more than the attacking patterns. Once
you know f7 is the target, the defensive moves stop looking arbitrary.

concepts.name: Opposition
concepts.one_liner: In king-and-pawn endings, the king that does not have to move wins the square.
concepts.teaching:
When the two kings face each other with one square between them, whoever is
*to move* must give way. Having the opposition means it is the opponent's
turn in that standoff.

This is the fundamental idea of king-and-pawn endgames. It converts a
question about squares into a question about turn parity, and it decides an
enormous number of otherwise identical-looking positions.

Beyond the direct opposition there is distant opposition, where the kings
stand an odd number of squares apart on a file, rank, or diagonal — the same
parity argument at a distance.

examples.caption: Black to move, so White holds the opposition. Black must step aside, White's king advances to the sixth rank in front of the pawn, and the pawn promotes. Won for White.

The identical position with White to move. Now White must give way, Black takes the opposition in reply, and the pawn never gets through. Drawn — the only difference between winning and drawing here is whose turn it is.

concepts.name: The Lucena Position
concepts.one_liner: The winning technique in rook-and-pawn endings — build a bridge.
concepts.teaching:
The most important winning position in rook endgames. Your pawn is on the
seventh, your king stands in front of it, and the enemy king is cut off — but
your own king is in the pawn's way and steps out into a barrage of checks.

The solution is "building a bridge": place your rook on the fourth rank so
that when the checks come, the rook can interpose and block one, ending the
checking sequence and freeing the king.

Rook endings are the most common endings in chess, and this is the position
they most often reduce to. Knowing it converts a large class of games that
otherwise drift into draws.

examples.caption: The Lucena position. White's king is in front of the pawn but blocking it, and stepping out invites endless checks. The winning idea is to build a bridge — the rook comes to the fourth rank so it can interpose against the checks.

concepts.name: The Philidor Position
concepts.one_liner: The drawing technique in rook-and-pawn endings — hold the third rank.
concepts.teaching:
The defensive counterpart to Lucena, and the more useful of the two, because
you will be worse more often than winning.

With your king in front of the enemy pawn, put your rook on your third rank
and keep it there. This stops the enemy king from advancing to the sixth. The
moment the pawn advances to the sixth itself, the rook swings to the eighth
rank and checks from behind — the pawn now blocks its own king from
sheltering, and the checks never end.

Two ideas, one rank each. Together they decide most rook endgames a club
player will ever reach.

examples.caption: The Philidor drawing method: the defending rook sits on its third rank to keep the enemy king off the sixth. Once the pawn advances to the sixth, the rook drops behind and checks forever.

concepts.name: Zugzwang
concepts.one_liner: Every legal move makes the position worse — and passing is not allowed.
concepts.teaching:
Chess has no pass. Zugzwang is the situation where a player would be fine if
they could simply do nothing, but every available move loses.

It is mostly an endgame phenomenon, because with few pieces there are few
harmless moves. In the middlegame there is nearly always something neutral
to play; in a king-and-pawn ending there may be nothing at all.

Zugzwang is also why the opposition works — the losing side is in zugzwang
and must step aside. And it is the reason engines and humans evaluate some
positions so differently: an engine has no trouble seeing that a position is
lost only because it is your turn.

concepts.name: Passed Pawn
concepts.one_liner: A pawn with no enemy pawn able to stop it must be watched every move.
concepts.teaching:
A passed pawn has no enemy pawn on its file or on either adjacent file. It
can only be stopped by a piece — which means it permanently ties down a
piece to babysit it.

Its value grows with every rank. On the fifth it is a nuisance, on the
seventh it decides games, and a piece that must sit and watch it is a piece
not participating anywhere else. That is the real point: a passed pawn wins
material indirectly by reducing the opponent's effective force.

Nimzowitsch's advice remains the best summary: a passed pawn is a criminal
that should be kept under lock and key — and, when it is yours, must be
pushed.

concepts.name: King Activity
concepts.one_liner: Once the queens are gone, the king is a strong piece — use it.
concepts.teaching:
Through the opening and middlegame the king is a liability to be hidden. In
the endgame that reverses completely: with few pieces left, the king is
worth roughly a minor piece in fighting strength, and the side whose king
reaches the centre first is usually just better.

This reversal is the single hardest habit for improving players to acquire,
because it directly contradicts everything correctly drilled about safety.
The tell is the queens coming off — after that, the king should be marching.

A great many endgames that look equal in material are decided entirely by
which king got to the centre first.

examples.caption: Material is dead level, yet White is much better purely because the king is already marching to the centre while Black's sits at home behind its pawns. In a queenless position the king is worth about a minor piece, and here only one side is using it.

concepts.name: Pawn Endgame Technique
concepts.one_liner: With only kings and pawns, calculation is exact and mistakes are fatal.
concepts.teaching:
King-and-pawn endgames are the one part of chess where evaluation is often a
matter of counting rather than judgement. Positions are either won, drawn, or
lost, and the difference is frequently a single tempo.

That makes them unforgiving. There are no pieces left to generate
compensation, so an error is not something you play around — it is the
result.

It also makes them learnable in a way the middlegame is not. The square of
the pawn, opposition, key squares, and triangulation between them settle most
positions, and each is a rule rather than an instinct.

concepts.name: Rook Activity
concepts.one_liner: An active rook is worth a pawn — often more.
concepts.teaching:
Rook endings are the most common endings in chess and the most frequently
misplayed. The governing principle is simple to state and hard to obey:
activity beats material.

A rook behind a passed pawn — yours or theirs — is doing real work. A rook
tied to defending a pawn is barely a piece at all. Given the choice between
holding a pawn passively and giving it up for an active rook on the seventh,
the active rook is usually correct.

This is why so many "winning" rook endings are drawn. The extra pawn was
bought with a passive rook, and the passive rook was worth more than the pawn.

examples.caption: Level material, but the rooks are not comparable. White's sits on the seventh attacking three pawns and cutting the king off; Black's is stuck on the back rank with no open file to enter. Activity is the currency of rook endings.

concepts.name: Pawn Structure
concepts.one_liner: Pawns cannot move backwards, so every pawn move is permanent.
concepts.teaching:
Pawns are the only pieces that cannot retreat. Every pawn move is therefore
a permanent commitment, and the resulting structure is the most durable
feature of a position — pieces come and go, the structure persists.

It determines almost everything else: which files open for rooks, which
squares are permanently safe for knights, which bishop is good and which is
bad, and where each side should be trying to play.

Philidor's claim that pawns are the soul of chess is not romanticism. It is
a statement about permanence. Choose the structure and you have chosen the
plan.

examples.caption: A Queen's Gambit Declined. Neither side has a weakness yet, but the pawn skeleton already dictates the plans: White plays on the queenside and in the centre, Black must free the light-squared bishop.

concepts.name: The Isolated Queen's Pawn
concepts.one_liner: A weakness in the endgame and an asset in the middlegame — the whole game turns on which.
concepts.teaching:
An isolated pawn has no friendly pawns on adjacent files, so no pawn can ever
defend it. The isolated d-pawn is the most studied example in chess.

It is simultaneously a weakness and a strength, which is what makes it such a
good teacher. The pawn itself is a permanent target and the square in front
of it is a permanent outpost for the opponent. In exchange, it grips two
central squares, opens two files for the rooks, and gives its owner freer
piece play.

That produces one of the clearest strategic dichotomies in chess: the side
with the isolated pawn wants pieces on and must attack; the side against it
wants to trade everything and reach an endgame. Both sides are right.

examples.caption: The classic isolated queen's pawn. White's d4 pawn has no pawn on the c- or e-file to defend it, so it is a permanent target — but it grips c5 and e5, and both White rooks have open files. White must play for the attack; Black wants to trade pieces and win the pawn in an endgame.

concepts.name: Doubled Pawns
concepts.one_liner: Usually a weakness, sometimes exactly what you wanted.
concepts.teaching:
Two pawns on the same file cannot defend each other and cannot easily create
a passed pawn. That is the standard case against them, and it is normally
right, especially heading into an endgame.

But they come with compensation that is easy to undervalue. Doubling
generally means capturing toward the centre, which opens a file for a rook
and adds central control. In several respectable openings a player accepts
doubled pawns deliberately for exactly that.

The useful question is never "are doubled pawns bad?" It is whether the
open file and the extra centre pawn are worth more than the structural
damage in the endgame you are heading for.

examples.caption: The Exchange Ruy Lopez. Black's doubled c-pawns can never make a passed pawn on the queenside, which is why White's whole plan is to reach an endgame — but Black gets the bishop pair and a half-open d-file as compensation.

concepts.name: Backward Pawn
concepts.one_liner: A pawn left behind on a half-open file is a target that cannot run.
concepts.teaching:
A backward pawn has fallen behind its neighbours, cannot advance safely, and
cannot be defended by another pawn. When it sits on a half-open file it
becomes a long-term target, because rooks can be stacked against something
that is unable to move.

The square directly in front of it is often the bigger problem. That square
can never be attacked by a pawn, making it a permanent home for an enemy
knight.

Backward pawns are usually created voluntarily, in exchange for activity.
Whether that trade was good is one of the more genuinely difficult
evaluations in chess.

examples.caption: A Najdorf where Black has just played e5. The d6 pawn is now backward on a half-open file — it cannot advance safely and no pawn can defend it — and the d5 square in front of it is a permanent home for a white piece. Black accepts both for control of the centre and active play.

concepts.name: Outpost
concepts.one_liner: A square no enemy pawn can ever attack, ideally occupied by a knight.
concepts.teaching:
An outpost is a square in or near enemy territory that cannot be challenged
by a pawn, because the pawns that would have done so are gone or have already
passed by.

A knight on a good outpost is often the strongest piece on the board. It
cannot be driven away by anything cheap, it attacks from a distance no other
piece can imitate, and it can only be dislodged by trading a piece of equal
or greater value — usually a concession in itself.

Finding them is a matter of reading the pawn structure rather than the
pieces. Look for squares the enemy pawns can no longer cover, then work out
how to get a knight there.

examples.caption: The white knight on e5 is a textbook outpost. Black's d- and f-pawns have both advanced past it and pawns cannot move backwards, so no pawn will ever attack e5 again. The knight can only be removed by giving up a piece of equal value for it.

concepts.name: The Open File
concepts.one_liner: Rooks need open files, and the seventh rank is the reward.
concepts.teaching:
Rooks are nearly worthless behind their own pawns and dominant on open
lines. Since an open file is usually the only route into the enemy position,
control of one is worth fighting for directly.

The fight is stereotyped enough to be a plan in itself: put a rook on the
file, double with the second rook or the queen, contest any enemy rook that
arrives, and use the file to invade — typically on the seventh rank, where a
rook attacks pawns still on their starting squares and confines the king.

Two rooks on the seventh are frequently decisive on their own, regardless of
material.

examples.caption: The Greco Attack, where the e-file has been swept clean. Whoever gets a rook there first — and White is about to — has the only route into the opponent's position.

concepts.name: The Bishop Pair
concepts.one_liner: Two bishops cover every square on the board; one covers half.
concepts.teaching:
A single bishop is permanently confined to one colour. Two bishops between
them see everything, and the pair is generally reckoned worth about half a
pawn more than bishop-and-knight or two knights.

The advantage is positional and slow. It grows as the position opens and as
material comes off, because bishops gain range while knights lose their
footholds. In a blocked position with fixed pawns, the pair may be worth
nothing at all, and a knight with a good outpost may be the better piece.

So possessing the pair implies a plan: open the position, trade pawns, head
for an endgame. Playing for the pair and then keeping the position closed is
a common and self-defeating mistake.

examples.caption: A Nimzo-Indian where Black has traded the dark-squared bishop for a knight. White holds the bishop pair and will try to open the position; Black will keep it closed and aim for a knight outpost.

concepts.name: Good and Bad Bishops
concepts.one_liner: A bishop blocked by its own pawns is barely a piece.
concepts.teaching:
A bishop is "bad" when its own pawns sit on its colour, blocking the
diagonals it needs. It is "good" when its pawns sit on the opposite colour,
leaving it free.

This is entirely a function of the pawn structure, which means it is
long-lasting and often decided many moves before anyone notices. It also
means it can be planned for: place your pawns on the colour opposite your
remaining bishop.

A worthwhile nuance — a bad bishop is not always a bad piece. If it is
defending the pawns that block it, it may be doing essential work. The
genuinely bad bishop is the one that is both blocked and useless, and the
standard remedy is to trade it or manoeuvre it outside the pawn chain.

examples.caption: Both sides have one bishop. Black's sits on the same colour as its own fixed pawns on d5 and c6 and is biting on granite; White's has open diagonals because the white pawns sit on dark squares only where the bishop is not. Same material, very different pieces.

concepts.name: Minority Attack
concepts.one_liner: Advance two pawns against three to manufacture a weakness.
concepts.teaching:
It seems backwards: attacking with fewer pawns than the defender has. The
goal is not to win material or break through, but to force an exchange that
leaves the defender with a permanent weakness.

The standard setting is the Carlsbad structure, where White pushes the b-pawn
to b5 against Black's a-, b-, and c-pawns. When it is exchanged, Black is
left with a backward c-pawn on a half-open file — precisely the target from
the backward-pawn concept — and White has a clear plan for the next twenty
moves.

It is the cleanest demonstration in chess that a plan can be about creating
a target rather than attacking an existing one.

examples.caption: The Carlsbad structure with White's rook swinging to b1. The plan is b4-b5, sending two pawns against three, purely to force an exchange that leaves Black with a backward c-pawn on a half-open file.

concepts.name: Prophylaxis
concepts.one_liner: Ask what your opponent wants, then make sure they cannot have it.
concepts.teaching:
Prophylaxis is preventing the opponent's plan rather than pursuing your own.
Nimzowitsch named it, and Karpov built a career on it.

In practice it is a question you ask every move: if it were their turn, what
would they play? Then consider stopping it. The resulting moves often look
like they do nothing — an unremarkable king move, a pawn nudge — and their
value is entirely in what never happens.

It is difficult to learn because there is no feedback. A prophylactic move
that works produces no visible event; the attack that was coming simply never
arrives, and it never looks like your move was the reason.

examples.caption: Black's only real freeing idea is ...e5 or ...c5. A prophylactic move — Rd1, adding a defender to d4 before anything is attacked — takes both breaks away. Nothing appears to happen, which is the point.

concepts.name: Space
concepts.one_liner: More space means more squares for your pieces and fewer for theirs.
concepts.teaching:
Advanced pawns claim territory. Behind them your pieces manoeuvre freely
while the opponent's get in each other's way, and a cramped position is hard
to play precisely because good squares are scarce.

Two rules follow, and they are among the most reliable in chess. The side
with more space should avoid exchanges, since every trade relieves the
cramp and leaves the remaining defenders more room. The cramped side should
seek exchanges for exactly the same reason.

Space is also a liability if overextended: advanced pawns cannot retreat, and
the squares behind them are permanently weak. It is an advantage that must be
used before it becomes a target.

examples.caption: A King's Indian where White has closed the centre with d5. White owns more of the board and should avoid trades; Black is cramped and wants them — and will counterattack on the kingside where the extra space matters least.

concepts.name: The Initiative
concepts.one_liner: Forcing the opponent to answer you is worth material.
concepts.teaching:
The initiative belongs to the player making threats — the one whose opponent
must spend every move responding rather than doing what they want.

It is temporary, unlike a structural advantage, and that is the key to
handling it. An initiative that is not converted into something permanent —
material, structure, king safety — evaporates, and the tempo spent acquiring
it is gone. This is why sacrificing for the initiative demands urgency: the
clock is running from the moment the material leaves.

It also explains why the defender's best practical move is often a
counter-threat rather than a defence. Answering threats forever loses; the
way out is to hand the problem back.

examples.caption: The Evans Gambit. White has given a pawn and in return every white move comes with a threat, so Black never gets a free move to consolidate. If the initiative is not converted before it fades, White is simply a pawn down.

concepts.name: Weak Squares and Colour Complexes
concepts.one_liner: A square no pawn can defend is a permanent hole.
concepts.teaching:
A weak square is one that can no longer be attacked by any pawn. Because
pawns cannot move backwards, the weakness is permanent — nothing later in the
game can repair it.

Individual holes matter, but the important case is a whole colour complex.
When several squares of one colour go weak at once — usually after the
bishop of that colour has been traded and pawns have settled on the other
colour — enemy pieces get a network of safe squares to hop between, and the
defence has nothing that can touch them.

Fianchettoing and then trading the fianchettoed bishop is the most common way
players do this to themselves.

examples.caption: Black has traded the dark-squared bishop off. With the g7 bishop gone and the black pawns fixed on dark squares, the squares around the black king are a colour complex nothing can defend.

concepts.name: The Exchange Sacrifice
concepts.one_liner: Give a rook for a minor piece to win squares, structure, or a bishop.
concepts.teaching:
Giving up a rook for a knight or bishop costs about a pawn and a half of
nominal material. It is a positional sacrifice: the return is not a
combination but a lasting feature of the position.

Typical reasons are worth listing, because they recur. Destroying the pawn
structure in front of a king. Eliminating a defender of a colour complex.
Winning a permanent outpost. Or simply that the rook had no open file and
the knight was the better piece anyway.

Petrosian made this an ordinary tool rather than a brilliancy, and his games
are the best demonstration that material tables are approximations rather
than facts.

examples.caption: The standard Sicilian exchange sacrifice shape: ...Rxc3 gives a rook for a knight to wreck White's queenside pawns and hand Black permanent control of the dark squares. Material says Black is worse; the position says otherwise.
